text:
CYRANO:
  No, no, my dear love, I did not love you!

ROXANE:
  Ah! How many things have died... how many have been born!
  —Why did you remain silent for fourteen years,
  Since, upon this letter in which he had no part,
  Those tears were yours?

CYRANO (holding out the letter to her):
  That blood was his.

ROXANE:
  Then why let that sublime silence
  Be broken today?

CYRANO:
  Why?...
  (Le Bret and Ragueneau run in.)



Scene 5.VI.

The same, Le Bret and Ragueneau.


LE BRET:
  What recklessness!
  Ah! I was certain of it! He is here!

CYRANO (smiling and straightening up):
  Well, by God!

LE BRET:
  He has killed himself, Madame, by getting up!

ROXANE:
  Great God!
  But just now, then... that weakness?... that?...

CYRANO:
  That is true! I had not finished my gazette:
  ...And on Saturday the twenty-sixth, one hour before dinner,
  Monsieur de Bergerac died by assassination.
  (He removes his hat; his head is seen wrapped in bandages.)

ROXANE:
  What is he saying?—Cyrano!—His head bandaged!...
  Ah, what have they done to you? Why?

CYRANO:
  “Struck by a hero with a sword,
  To fall with its point in my heart!”...
  —Yes, that is what I used to say!... Fate is mocking!...
  And now I am killed in an ambush,
  From behind, by a lackey, with a blow from a log!
  That is just fine. I shall have failed in everything, even my death.

RAGUENEAU:
  Ah, Monsieur!...

CYRANO:
  Ragueneau, do not cry so hard!...
  (He holds out his hand to him.)
  What has become of thee now, my fellow craftsman?

RAGUENEAU (through his tears):
  I am a snuffer of... of... candles, in Molière’s company.

CYRANO:
  Molière!

RAGUENEAU:
  But I mean to leave him tomorrow:
  Yes, I am indignant!... Yesterday they were performing Scapin,
  And I saw that he had taken a scene from you!

LE BRET:
  A whole one!

RAGUENEAU:
  Yes, Monsieur, the famous: “What the devil was he doing?...”

LE BRET (furiously):
  Molière took it from thee!

CYRANO:
  Hush! Hush! He did well!...
  (To Ragueneau.)
  The scene has a great effect, does it not?

RAGUENEAU (sobbing):
  Ah! Monsieur, they laughed! They laughed!

CYRANO:
  Yes, my life
  Has been to be the one who prompts—and whom they forget!
  (To Roxane.)
  Do you remember the evening when Christian spoke to you
  Beneath the balcony? Well! My entire life is there:
  While I remained below, in the black shadow,
  Others climbed up to gather glory’s kiss!
  It is just, and I approve upon the threshold of my tomb:
  Molière has genius, and Christian was handsome!
  (At that moment, the chapel bell having rung, the nuns can be seen
  passing in the background, along the path, on their way to the service.)
  Let them go and pray, since their bell is ringing!

ROXANE (rising to call out):
  Sister! Sister!

CYRANO (restraining her):
  No! No! Do not go and fetch anyone:
  Even if you came back, I would no longer be here.
  (The nuns have entered the chapel; the organ is heard.)
  I was lacking a little harmony... there it is.

ROXANE:
  I love you; live!

CYRANO:
  No! For it is in the fairy tale
  That when one says, “I love thee!” to the shame-filled prince,
  He feels his ugliness melt at those sunlit words...
  But thou wouldst notice that I remain the same.

ROXANE:
  I have caused your unhappiness! I! I!

CYRANO:
  You?... On the contrary!
  I did not know feminine tenderness. My mother
  Did not find me handsome. I had no sister.
  Later, I feared the mistress with the mocking eye.
  I owe it to you that I had, at least, a woman friend.
  Thanks to you, a gown passed through my life.

LE BRET (showing him the moonlight descending through the branches):
  Thy other friend is there, coming to see thee!

CYRANO (smiling at the moon):
  I see.

ROXANE:
  I loved only one being, and I lose him twice!

CYRANO:
  Le Bret, I am going to ascend into the opaline moon,
  With no need today to invent a machine...

LE BRET:
  What are you saying?

CYRANO:
  Why, yes, it is there, I tell you,
  That they are going to send me to make my paradise.
  More than one soul I love must be exiled there,
  And I shall find Socrates and Galileo again!

LE BRET (protesting):
  No, no! It is too stupid, after all, and too
  Unjust! Such a poet! A heart so great, so noble!
  To die like this!... To die!...

CYRANO:
  There is Le Bret growling!

LE BRET (bursting into tears):
  My dear friend...

CYRANO (raising himself, his eyes wandering):
  They are the Cadets of Gascony...
  —Elementary mass... Why, yes!... there is the rub...

LE BRET:
  His science... in his delirium!

CYRANO:
  Copernicus
  Said...

ROXANE:
  Oh!

CYRANO:
  But also, what the devil was he doing,
  What the devil was he doing in that galley?...
  Philosopher, physicist,
  Rhymer, swordsman, musician,
  And traveler through the air,
  Great master of the swift retort,
  Lover too—not for his own good!—
  Here lies Hercule-Savinien
  De Cyrano de Bergerac,
  Who was everything, and who was nothing,
  ...But I am leaving; forgive me, I cannot keep them waiting:
  You see, the moonbeam is coming to take me!
  (He falls back into a sitting position; Roxane’s tears recall him to reality.
  He looks at her and caresses her veils.)
  I do not want you to mourn any less for that charming,
  That good, that handsome Christian; but I want only
  That when the great cold has seized my vertebrae,
  You give a double meaning to those mourning veils,
  And that your mourning for him become, a little, mourning for me.

ROXANE:
  I swear it to you!...

CYRANO (shaken by a great shudder and rising abruptly):
  Not there! No! Not in that armchair!
  (They try to rush toward him.)
  —Do not support me!—No one!
  (He goes and braces himself against the tree.)
  Nothing but the tree!
  (Silence.)
  She is coming. I already feel myself booted in marble,
  —Gloved in lead!
  (He stiffens.)
  Oh! But... since she is on her way,
  I shall await her standing,
  (He draws his sword.)
  And with sword in hand!

LE BRET:
  Cyrano!

ROXANE (fainting):
  Cyrano!
  (All recoil in terror.)

CYRANO:
  I believe she is looking...
  That she dares to look at my nose, that Snub-Nosed One!
  (He raises his sword.)
  What do you say?... It is useless?... I know!
  But one does not fight in the hope of success!
  No! No! It is far finer when it is useless!
  —Who are all those?—Are there a thousand of you?
  Ah! I recognize you, all my old enemies!
  Falsehood?
  (He strikes the empty air with his sword.)
  Take that, take that!—Ha! Ha! Compromises!
  Prejudices, Cowardices!...
  (He strikes.)
  That I should make terms?
  Never, never!—Ah! There thou art, Folly!
  —I know full well that in the end you will strike me down;
  No matter: I fight! I fight! I fight!
  (He makes immense sweeping strokes and stops, gasping.)
  Yes, you tear everything from me, the laurel and the rose!
  Tear them away! In spite of you, there is something
  That I carry with me, and tonight, when I enter God’s house,
  My salute will sweep broadly across the blue threshold,
  Something that, without a crease, without a stain,
  I carry with me in spite of you,
  (He springs forward, sword held high.)
  And it is...
  (The sword slips from his hands; he staggers and falls into the arms of
  Le Bret and Ragueneau.)
